title: Continual Concept Personalization in Diffusion Models via Residual-Space Adaptation

paper.title: Continual Concept Personalization in Diffusion Models via Residual-Space Adaptation
paper.abstract: Abstract Text-to-image personalization aims to equip pretrained diffusion models with the ability to learn user-specific concepts from only a few reference images. Existing methods, however, typically train each concept independently or assume that all concepts are available simultaneously. In practical applications, concepts often arrive sequentially, requiring models to continually learn new subjects, objects, or styles while minimizing interference with previously acquired concepts. We address this continual concept personalization setting by extending residual-space adaptation to the stochastic adaptation process of pretrained diffusion models. Our work achieves the highest concept fidelity among competing continual personalization methods while maintaining near-zero forgetting. Beyond these empirical gains, the learned residual-space dynamics reveal where adaptation capacity is concentrated within the diffusion model. Restricting adaptation to the identified layers preserves nearly the same performance while reducing the number of trainable parameters by up to 72%, demonstrating that residual-space dynamics can identify the layers that contribute most to continual concept personalization and directly guide more parameter-efficient adaptation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent text-to-image models such as Stable Diffusion [ 17 , 15 ] and FLUX [ 11 ] have enabled high-quality image synthesis from natural language descriptions, making generative models increasingly accessible to end users. Their flexibility has further motivated personalization methods that adapt pretrained models to user-specific concepts, subjects, objects, or artistic styles from only a few examples. Personalization methods commonly rely on parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques such as LoRA [ 9 ] to adapt pretrained diffusion models to new concepts. Most existing approaches [ 7 , 14 , 10 , 21 ] perform a separate fine-tuning procedure for every concept, and subsequently merge the resulting adapters into a unified personalized model. In many practical scenarios, however, concepts are acquired sequentially over time as new subjects, objects, or styles become available. Under this setting, whenever a new concept is introduced, the expensive merging procedure must be repeated to reconstruct the final personalized model. As the number of concepts grows, this repeated merging process becomes increasingly inefficient. This motivates continual concept personalization, where a single model is updated incrementally to incorporate new concepts while preserving previously acquired ones. The main obstacle to continual concept personalization is interference: learning new concepts can degrade performance on previously learned concepts. At the same time, the fixed model capacity must be used parsimoniously to preserve sufficient adaptation capacity for future concepts. Several continual learning methods [ 4 , 19 , 12 , 1 ] achieve low levels of interference by constraining the parameter update to a pre-computed safe subspace. The most successful among these rely on layer-wise input statistics to characterize the safe subspace. This procedure cannot be directly extended to stochastic backbones, thus limiting its applicability in image generation tasks. In this work, we bridge this gap, extending residual-space adaptation to stochastic diffusion models for continual concept personalization. In particular, our starting point is an adapted version of DyRA [ 1 ] into diffusion models, a recent method which we choose for its elegant formulation and explicit theoretical guarantees. We also introduce a novel systematic evaluation framework for continual concept personalization and show that the resulting residual-space dynamics reveal layerwise specialization, providing a practical tool for guiding parameter-efficient adaptation.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our contributions are as follows: • We extend residual-space adaptation from deterministic language models to stochastic diffusion training, providing a new competitive option for continual concept personalization that mitigates interference while maintaining adaptivity at low cost. • We introduce a systematic evaluation framework for continual personalization that captures concept fidelity, going beyond judging only image-generation quality. • We show that residual-space dynamics can serve as an efficient probe for identifying the layers that contribute most to continual concept adaptation, providing insights into layerwise specialization and guiding more targeted parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies.

sections.heading: 2.1 Diffusion Personalization
sections.text: Text-to-image personalization has been widely studied for adapting pretrained diffusion models to user-specific identities, objects, or styles from only a few examples. Early approaches such as Textual Inversion [ 6 ] learn new concepts in the text embedding space while keeping the diffusion model fixed. DreamBooth [ 18 ] improves personalization quality by fine-tuning the diffusion model using a prior-preservation objective. Subsequent methods such as Custom Diffusion [ 10 ] restrict adaptation to selected cross-attention layers, improving parameter efficiency while supporting multi-concept customization. More recent personalization methods increasingly adopt parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques such as LoRA. Mix-of-Show [ 7 ] introduces ED-LoRA together with structured concept tokens for multi-concept personalization, while LoRACLR [ 21 ] improves composition through contrastive alignment of independently trained adapters. Another line of work reduces interference through the design of the adaptation space itself. Orthogonal Adaptation (OA) [ 14 ] constructs approximately orthogonal LoRA subspaces, allowing independently trained adapters to be combined through simple summation with minimal interference. Although originally proposed in a non-continual setting, its orthogonal structure naturally lends itself to sequential adaptation. Overall, most existing personalization methods assume that all concepts are jointly available during training or are learned independently and combined afterward, and are therefore not explicitly designed for continual settings.

sections.heading: 2.2 Continual Adaptation
sections.text: Continual learning methods [ 8 ] operate in a sequential training fashion, aiming to preserve knowledge and plasticity over time. Classical approaches rely on regularization, replay, or gradient projection mechanisms to mitigate catastrophic forgetting [ 23 ] . Within diffusion adaptation, C-LoRA [ 22 ] extends Custom Diffusion to a sequential setting by introducing regularization to preserve earlier concepts. Orthogonal Adaptation [ 14 ] can also be naturally extended to continual settings through additive composition of orthogonal adapters. Several methods constrain the parameter update to a safe subspace based on the layer-wise input statistics. Among these, Gradient Projection Memory (GPM) [ 19 ] estimates layer-wise feature covariance from previous tasks and constrains the new updates to its low-energy subspace. The more recent InfLoRA [ 12 ] applies the same strategy to LoRA-based fine-tuning, where each task is learned within a fixed low-rank budget. Building upon InfLoRA, Barinka et al. [ 1 ] propose a dynamic rank allocation method with simplified updates which allows for significant capacity savings. In addition to providing theoretical guarantees for mitigating forgetting, the method demonstrates strong empirical performance on challenging continual language model adaptation tasks. Although effective, these approaches have been studied primarily in deterministic architectures. Whether residual-space methods remain effective in stochastic diffusion training, where layer statistics are influenced by sampled noise, remains unexplored.

sections.heading: 2.3 Evaluation of Personalized Generative Models
sections.text: Evaluating personalized generative models typically involves measuring text alignment, image similarity, and identity preservation. Text alignment is commonly assessed using CLIP-based [ 16 ] text-image similarity, which measures whether generated images are semantically consistent with their prompts. Image alignment metrics compare generated images with reference examples, often using CLIP image embeddings. Several works additionally evaluate identity preservation through specialized recognition models such as ArcFace [ 3 ] . However, these metrics are mainly designed for human faces and do not generalize to arbitrary objects. Beyond specialized identity metrics, a variety of pretrained embedding models have been used to assess perceptual similarity. CLIP [ 16 ] is trained on large-scale image–text pairs and provides representations that emphasize global semantic correspondence between images and language. In contrast, DINO-based models [ 2 , 13 , 20 ] learn self-supervised visual representations without text supervision and preserve fine-grained visual structure and local semantic information. DreamSim [ 5 ] combines multiple pretrained visual embeddings together with human similarity annotations, leveraging both global semantic understanding and fine-grained visual details to produce perceptual representations that closely align with human judgments. Overall, most existing evaluation protocols are designed for static personalization settings and do not measure identity preservation or forgetting over time.

sections.heading: 3 Evaluating Continual Performance
sections.text: Evaluating continual text-to-image personalization requires measuring not only the quality of generated images but also how well previously learned concepts are preserved throughout sequential adaptation. Unlike discriminative tasks, where forgetting can be directly quantified through accuracy, there is no canonical notion of forgetting for generative models. As discussed in Section 2.3 , existing evaluation protocols are primarily designed for static personalization settings and focus on aggregate measures of text or image alignment. In order to assess the degradation of the concept identity over time, it is important to have metrics that distinguish concept fidelity from general image quality. To address this problem, we first introduce a concept-level fidelity measure that quantifies how faithfully a personalized concept is preserved. We then derive continual evaluation metrics directly from this quantity.

sections.heading: 3.1 Concept Fidelity
sections.text: Our objective is to evaluate the personalized concept itself rather than the similarity between individual images. A generated image may differ substantially from its reference in pose, background, or artistic style while still faithfully depicting the same concept. We therefore introduce concept fidelity , which measures similarity at the concept level rather than the image level. To quantify concept fidelity, we first measure similarity between individual generated and reference images in a learned embedding space. We therefore generalize the image-level similarity measure by aggregating pairwise similarities across the generated and reference image sets. sections.heading: 4 Residual-Space Adaptation in Diffusion
sections.text: We build upon the residual-space adaptation framework DyRA [ 1 ] , originally designed for LLMs, which constructs layer-wise adaptation subspaces from the input representations. Applying this framework to diffusion models is nontrivial, as these representations depend not only on the input concept but also on the randomly sampled diffusion noise and denoising timestep. We therefore first review the residual-space adaptation procedure and then develop a stochastic interpretation that justifies applying the framework to diffusion models and motivates our implementation.

sections.heading: 4.1 Background: DyRA
sections.text: We consider a sequence of concept personalization tasks { 𝒟 t } t = 1 T \{\mathcal{D}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} , where each task introduces a new concept t t and training is performed sequentially. Following [ 1 ] , each adapted layer l l is parameterized by a LoRA update Δ ​ W t ( l ) = A t ( l ) ​ B t ( l ) , \Delta W_{t}^{(l)}=A_{t}^{(l)}B_{t}^{(l)}, (6) where B t ( l ) B_{t}^{(l)} is initialized before training and kept fixed, while only A t ( l ) A_{t}^{(l)} is optimized. The accumulated model after task t t is W t ( l ) = W ( l ) + ∑ i = 1 t Δ ​ W i ( l ) . W_{t}^{(l)}=W^{(l)}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}\Delta W_{i}^{(l)}. (7) The key idea of DyRA is to restrict learning to feature directions that are informative for the current task while avoiding directions already captured by previous tasks. For each adapted layer, the method applies a spectral decomposition of the input features matrix from all tasks, and identifies therein directions unique to the current task, i.e. the residual space leftover from previous tasks. Since different layers exhibit different residual-space spectra, the number of informative directions also varies, motivating adaptive rank allocation instead of a fixed LoRA rank. Concretely, the procedure for each adapted layer consists of three steps: 1. Estimate the input subspace most representative of previous tasks, named ℳ t − 1 ( l ) \mathcal{M}_{t-1}^{(l)} . 2. Project the current task input space ℋ t ( l ) \mathcal{H}_{t}^{(l)} onto the orthogonal complement of ℳ t − 1 ( l ) \mathcal{M}_{t-1}^{(l)} to obtain the residual space. 3. Initialize the LoRA down-projection matrix B t ( l ) B_{t}^{(l)} in the residual space, picking only directions with singular values above a given threshold τ \tau . During training, B t ( l ) B_{t}^{(l)} remains fixed and only the corresponding up-projection matrix A t ( l ) A_{t}^{(l)} is optimized. Importantly, it is the threshold which implicitly determines the layer-wise rank. This is the key to flexible rank allocation.

sections.heading: 4.2 A Stochastic Formulation for Diffusion
sections.text: A key step of residual-space adaptation is constructing the residual space from layer input representations collected before training each task. For deterministic backbones, this procedure is well defined since each training sample corresponds to a unique layer input. Diffusion models, however, introduce an additional source of stochasticity through the sampled diffusion noise and denoising timestep, so the layer input of a training sample is no longer unique. This raises the central question of this section: how should the layer input space ℋ t ( l ) \mathcal{H}_{t}^{(l)} be estimated for residual-space construction? This simple step extends residual-space adaptation from deterministic feature representations to stochastic diffusion training by aligning the feature collection procedure with the stochastic optimization objective. sections.heading: 5 Stable Continual Personalization
sections.text: This section evaluates whether residual-space adaptation can be successfully extended to continual diffusion personalization. We first assess its ability to preserve concept fidelity while mitigating forgetting throughout continual learning, and then examine scalability and capacity preservation.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We conduct all experiments on Concept101 [ 10 ] , a benchmark containing 101 concepts spanning 17 semantic classes, including visually similar concepts, making it particularly suitable for studying interference and identity preservation in continual learning. All concepts are learned sequentially in a rehearsal-free setting, where only the current concept data are available during training. Unless otherwise stated, all methods follow the same randomly shuffled task ordering. Throughout the experiments, we denote DyRA configured with the sigular value threshold τ \tau as DyRA- τ \tau . We compare DyRA with τ ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{0.5,1.0\} against three continual LoRA baselines: Trainable-AB , which optimizes both LoRA projection matrices A , B A,B and corresponds to a continual variant of Mix-of-Show [ 7 ] ; Rank-Fixed-B , which optimizes only the LoRA up-projection A A while keeping the randomly initialized down-projection B B fixed; and OA , the continual version of Orthogonal Adaptation [ 14 ] . Unless otherwise specified, all methods adapt the linear projections in the transformer blocks of both the text encoder and the UNet, and all fixed-rank methods use rank r = 4 r=4 . All experiments are conducted on Stable Diffusion v1.5 [ 17 ] . Models are periodically evaluated throughout continual training. For each concept, images are generated using only the learned concept token as the prompt, without additional textual descriptions, thereby isolating the learned concept representation and enabling a direct comparison of concept fidelity across methods. At the end of training, we further validate the model using diverse prompt templates. Additional implementation details and training hyperparameters are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 5.3 Dynamic Rank Improves Parameter Efficiency
sections.text: The performance gains of DyRA stem not only from restricting adaptation to the residual space, but also from allocating adaptation capacity according to the residual-space structure of each layer. We therefore compare DyRA with the fixed-rank OA under different trainable parameter budgets to evaluate the effectiveness of dynamic rank allocation. Figure 5 compares concept fidelity against the number of trainable parameters for OA with different fixed ranks and DyRA with different singular-value thresholds. Each point corresponds to a different parameter budget. Across the entire range of budgets, DyRA consistently achieves higher concept fidelity than OA with comparable numbers of trainable parameters, demonstrating a superior performance–parameter trade-off. Figure 5 : Parameter-efficiency frontier comparing concept fidelity and trainable parameter count for OA and DyRA variants. Error bars indicate one standard deviation over three random seeds. Notably, even under high singular-value thresholds, where DyRA has substantially fewer trainable parameters, it outperforms OA with considerably larger parameter budgets. These results indicate that allocating rank adaptively according to the residual-space structure is substantially more parameter-efficient than assigning a uniform rank to every layer, allowing DyRA to maintain strong concept fidelity under a reduced parameter budget.

sections.heading: 6 Layer-wise Specialization
sections.text: Section 5 demonstrated that DyRA achieves strong continual personalization performance while improving parameter efficiency through adaptive rank allocation. Beyond these empirical gains, the adaptive ranks themselves provide a signal of where adaptation capacity is consumed during continual learning, since additional rank is allocated only when new concepts introduce directions outside the accumulated input subspace. This section analyzes these rank dynamics to understand how adaptation capacity is distributed across the layers and how this information can inform future parameter-efficient adaptation.

sections.heading: 6.1 Adaptation Capacity Concentration
sections.text: We first analyze how DyRA distributes adaptation capacity across the adapted layers by averaging the allocated ranks over all 101 concepts. Figure 6 illustrates the average rank allocated to each layer. The x-axis indexes the adapted layers in architectural order, and the corresponding module names are provided in Appendix D . Rather than allocating the same rank to every layer, DyRA exhibits clear layer-dependent allocation patterns that closely follow the repeated transformer architecture. In the text encoder, the allocated ranks exhibit a four-layer periodicity that exactly mirrors the repeated key(K), value(V), query(Q), and output projection layers within each transformer block. A similar correspondence is observed in the UNet, where every group of eight adapted layers corresponds to the self-attention and cross-attention projections within a transformer block. Within every block, the two dominant rank peaks consistently coincide with the cross-attention key(K) and value(V) projection layers, which repeatedly receive substantially larger ranks than all other projections. The repeated concentration of residual rank in the UNet cross-attention K,V projections indicates that these layers consistently consume more adaptation capacity than other adapted modules during continual concept personalization. This observation motivates a closer examination of these layers in the following analysis. Figure 6 : Average allocated rank per adapted layer over 101 concepts.

sections.heading: 6.3 Layer-Guided Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
sections.text: The analyses in Sections 6.1 and 6.2 consistently identify the UNet cross-attention K,V projections as the layers that require the largest residual adaptation subspaces throughout continual learning. This suggests that these layers differentiate newly learned concepts through distinct adaptation directions. If this interpretation is correct, restricting adaptation to the identified layers would be expected to preserve most of the continual personalization performance while substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. Table 3 supports this hypothesis. Restricting adaptation to only the UNet K,V projections reduces the trainable parameter count by approximately 60% (67.56M → \rightarrow 27.12M) while achieving virtually identical concept fidelity ( Q = 0.6496 Q=0.6496 vs. 0.6497 0.6497 ) and comparable forgetting. Restricting adaptation further to only the UNet cross-attention K,V projections reduces the trainable parameter count by approximately 72% (67.56M → \rightarrow 18.87M), yet still preserves nearly all continual personalization performance in practice. Beyond validating the proposed interpretation, these results also provide a structural explanation for previous personalization methods such as Custom Diffusion [ 10 ] and C-LoRA [ 22 ] , which restrict adaptation to cross-attention K,V projections based primarily on empirical observations of large weight updates during training. In contrast, residual-space dynamics explain the same design choice from the perspective of feature-space utilization, providing a principled interpretation of why these layers are particularly effective adaptation targets. More broadly, residual-space dynamics provide a principled way to identify where adaptation capacity is most effectively utilized. Rather than relying on empirical heuristics or exhaustive layerwise search, the proposed analysis directly guides targeted adaptation, enabling substantially more parameter-efficient continual personalization while preserving nearly the same overall performance. sections.heading: Limitations and Future Directions.
sections.text: Although DyRA achieves strong continual personalization performance, several limitations remain. First, the adaptation capacity of residual-space methods is fundamentally bounded by the width of individual layers. As continual learning progresses, layers with consistently high adaptation demand may eventually exhaust their available residual subspaces, limiting scalability to arbitrarily long task sequences. Second, the method is implemented only on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and Concept101. Nevertheless, the residual-space analysis developed in this work is considerably more general than the specific adaptation algorithm. Since it relies only on layer input statistics and residual-space dynamics, it can potentially be applied to other diffusion backbones, transformer-based generative models, or broader neural architectures to identify the layers that contribute most to learning new tasks. Exploring these adaptation patterns across architectures may provide further insights into representation specialization and guide the design of future parameter-efficient adaptation methods.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways.
sections.text: Our work shows that residual-space adaptation extends naturally to stochastic diffusion models, enabling continual concept personalization with stable performance, negligible interference, and strong parameter efficiency. Beyond its empirical performance, the residual-space dynamics observed during continual adaptation reveal how adaptation demand is distributed across the adapted layers. By identifying the layers that consistently require new concept-specific adaptation directions, it provides a structural interpretation of existing adaptation strategies and directly guides more parameter-efficient adaptation. We hope this perspective motivates future work that uses adaptation dynamics not only to improve continual learning algorithms, but also to better understand layer specialization in modern generative models.

sections.heading: Appendix A Embedding Metric Comparison
sections.text: We quantitatively compare the embedding spaces used to compute concept fidelity in the main text. The goal of this comparison is to measure whether an embedding model captures concept-level identity rather than only low-level visual similarity. A suitable embedding should map images of the same personalized concept close to one another while separating images from different concepts. We evaluate this property using a clustering protocol on the ground-truth reference images. Given image embeddings, we define the pairwise clustering distance as d ⁡ ( i 1 , i 2 ) = 1 − sim ⁡ ( i 1 , i 2 ) , d(i_{1},i_{2})=1-\mathrm{sim}(i_{1},i_{2}), (10) where sim ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) \mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot) denotes the cosine similarity in the corresponding embedding space. We cluster all ground-truth images into 101 clusters, matching the number of personalized concepts. To make the comparison deterministic and reduce sensitivity to random initialization, the cluster centroids are initialized using one image from each ground-truth concept. We report clustering accuracy and Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) with respect to the ground-truth concept labels. Clustering accuracy is computed as the fraction of images assigned to their correct concept cluster. ARI measures the agreement between the predicted clustering and the ground-truth partition based on pairwise co-clustering decisions, adjusted for chance. Higher values indicate that the embedding space better recovers the underlying concept structure. Embedding model Acc. sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation Details
sections.text: We provide additional implementation details for the continual personalization experiments in the main text.

sections.heading: Dataset and task order.
sections.text: We randomly shuffle the 101 concepts once and use this fixed task order for all methods and random seeds in the main experiments. This avoids presenting concepts in semantic clusters, such as all visually similar instances from the same class arriving consecutively. During each task, the dataloader contains only the reference images for the current concept. To check robustness to task ordering, we additionally repeat all experiments with two other independently shuffled concept orders and observe results consistent with those reported in the main text.

sections.heading: Backbone and adapted layers.
sections.text: We use Stable Diffusion v1.5 [ 17 ] as the pretrained text-to-image backbone. The model uses a CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder with 12 transformer blocks and a UNet with 16 cross-attention blocks. LoRA modules are inserted into the query, key, value, and output projections of the attention layers in both the text encoder and the UNet. This yields 48 adapted projection layers in the text encoder and 128 adapted projection layers in the UNet.

sections.heading: Training configuration.
sections.text: Each concept is trained for 400 gradient-update steps. Since each concept has only a small number of reference images, the concept dataset is cycled during training. We train with fp16 mixed precision on two NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. All methods are run with three global random seeds, { 0 , 42 , 619 } \{0,42,619\} . sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We evaluate the model every 50 training steps. At each evaluation checkpoint, we generate images for all concepts that have been learned so far. For each concept, we sample 10 images using different random seeds. The generated images are compared with the ground-truth reference images using the concept-fidelity metric described in the main text. During this quantitative evaluation, we prompt the model only with the two concept-specific tokens, ⟨ c 1 ⟩ ​ ⟨ c 2 ⟩ \langle c_{1}\rangle\langle c_{2}\rangle , to isolate concept identity from prompt-induced scene variation.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.28567v1 [cs.CV] 20 Oct 2026 Continual Concept Personalization in Diffusion Models via Residual-Space Adaptation Yuzhi Liu † † thanks: Corresponding to: yuzliu@student.ethz.ch Enis Simsar Giulia Lanzillotta Thomas Hofmann Affiliation: ETH Zürich Abstract Text-to-image personalization aims to equip pretrained diffusion models with the ability to learn user-specific concepts from only a few reference images. Existing methods, however, typically train each concept independently or assume that all concepts are available simultaneously. In practical applications, concepts often arrive sequentially, requiring models to continually learn new subjects, objects, or styles while minimizing interference with previously acquired concepts. We address this continual concept personalization setting by extending residual-space adaptation to the stochastic adaptation process of pretrained diffusion models. Our work achieves the highest concept fidelity among competing continual personalization methods while maintaining near-zero forgetting. Beyond these empirical gains, the learned residual-space dynamics reveal where adaptation capacity is concentrated within the diffusion model. Restricting adaptation to the identified layers preserves nearly the same performance while reducing the number of trainable parameters by up to 72%, demonstrating that residual-space dynamics can identify the layers that contribute most to continual concept personalization and directly guide more parameter-efficient adaptation. 1 Introduction Recent text-to-image models such as Stable Diffusion [ 17 , 15 ] and FLUX [ 11 ] have enabled high-quality image synthesis from natural language descriptions, making generative models increasingly accessible to end users. Their flexibility has further motivated personalization methods that adapt pretrained models to user-specific concepts, subjects, objects, or artistic styles from only a few examples. Personalization methods commonly rely on parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques such as LoRA [ 9 ] to adapt pretrained diffusion models to new concepts. Most existing approaches [ 7 , 14 , 10 , 21 ] perform a separate fine-tuning procedure for every concept, and subsequently merge the resulting adapters into a unified personalized model. In many practical scenarios, however, concepts are acquired sequentially over time as new subjects, objects, or styles become available. Under this setting, whenever a new concept is introduced, the expensive merging procedure must be repeated to reconstruct the final personalized model. As the number of concepts grows, this repeated merging process becomes increasingly inefficient. This motivates continual concept personalization, where a single model is updated incrementally to incorporate new concepts while preserving previously acquired ones. The main obstacle to continual concept personalization is interference: learning new concepts can degrade performance on previously learned concepts. At the same time, the fixed model capacity must be used parsimoniously to preserve sufficient adaptation capacity for future concepts. Several continual learning methods [ 4 , 19 , 12 , 1 ] achieve low levels of interference by constraining the parameter update to a pre-computed safe subspace. The most successful among these rely on layer-wise input statistics to characterize the safe subspace. This procedure cannot be directly extended to stochastic backbones, thus limiting its applicability in image generation tasks. In this work, we bridge this gap, extending residual-space adaptation to stochastic diffusion models for continual concept personalization. In particular, our starting point is an adapted version of DyRA [ 1 ] into diffusion models, a recent method which we choose for its elegant formulation and explicit theoretical guarantees. We also introduce a novel systematic evaluation framework for continual concept personalization and show that the resulting residual-space dynamics reveal layerwise specialization, providing a practical tool for guiding parameter-efficient adaptation. Contributions. Our contributions are as follows: • We extend residual-space adaptation from deterministic language models to stochastic diffusion training, providing a new competitive option for continual concept personalization that mitigates interference while maintaining adaptivity at low cost. • We introduce a systematic evaluation framework for continual personalization that captures concept fidelity, going beyond judging only image-generation quality. • We show that residual-space dynamics can serve as an efficient probe for identifying the layers that contribute most to continual concept adaptation, providing insights into layerwise specialization and guiding more targeted parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies. 2 Related Work 2.1 Diffusion Personalization Text-to-image personalization has been widely studied for adapting pretrained diffusion models to user-specific identities, objects, or styles from only a few examples. Early approaches such as Textual Inversion [ 6 ] learn new concepts in the text embedding space while keeping the diffusion model fixed. DreamBooth [ 18 ] improves personalization quality by fine-tuning the diffusion model using a prior-preservation objective. Subsequent methods such as Custom Diffusion [ 10 ] restrict adaptation to selected cross-attention layers, improving parameter efficiency while supporting multi-concept customization. More recent personalization methods increasingly adopt parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques such as LoRA. Mix-of-Show [ 7 ] introduces ED-LoRA together with structured concept tokens for multi-concept personalization, while LoRACLR [ 21 ] improves composition through contrastive alignment of independently trained adapters. Another line of work reduces interference through the design of the adaptation space itself. Orthogonal Adaptation (OA) [ 14 ] constructs approximately orthogonal LoRA subspaces, allowing independently trained adapters to be combined through simple summation with minimal interference. Although originally proposed in a non-continual setting, its orthogonal structure naturally lends itself to sequential adaptation. Overall, most existing personalization methods assume that all concepts are jointly available during training or are learned independently and combined afterward, and are therefore not explicitly designed for continual settings. 2.2 Continual Adaptation Continual learning methods [ 8 ] operate in a sequential training fashion, aiming to preserve knowledge and plasticity over time. Classical approaches rely on regularization, replay, or gradient projection mechanisms to mitigate catastrophic forgetting [ 23 ] . Within diffusion adaptation, C-LoRA [ 22 ] extends Custom Diffusion to a sequential setting by introducing regularization to preserve earlier concepts. Orthogonal Adaptation [ 14 ] can also be naturally extended to continual settings through additive composition of orthogonal adapters. Several methods constrain the parameter update to a safe subspace based on the layer-wise input statistics. Among these, Gradient Projection Memory (GPM) [ 19 ] estimates layer-wise feature covariance from previous tasks and constrains the new updates to its low-energy subspace. The more recent InfLoRA [ 12 ] applies the same strategy to LoRA-based fine-tuning, where each task is learned within a fixed low-rank budget. Building upon InfLoRA, Barinka et al. [ 1 ] propose a dynamic rank allocation method with simplified updates which allows for significant capacity savings. In addition to providing theoretical guarantees for mitigating forgetting, the method demonstrates strong empirical performance on challenging continual language model adaptation tasks. Although effective, these approaches have been studied primarily in deterministic architectures. Whether residual-space methods remain effective in stochastic diffusion training, where layer statistics are influenced by sampled noise, remains unexplored. 2.3 Evaluation of Personalized Generative Models Evaluating personalized generative models typically involves measuring text alignment, image similarity, and identity preservation. Text alignment is commonly assessed using CLIP-based [ 16 ] text-image similarity, which measures whether generated images are semantically consistent with their prompts. Image alignment metrics compare generated images with reference examples, often using CLIP image embeddings. Several works additionally evaluate identity preservation through specialized recognition models such as ArcFace [ 3 ] . However, these metrics are mainly designed for human faces and do not generalize to arbitrary objects. Beyond specialized identity metrics, a variety of pretrained embedding models have been used to assess perceptual similarity. CLIP [ 16 ] is trained on large-scale image–text pairs and provides representations that emphasize global semantic correspondence between images and language. In contrast, DINO-based models [ 2 , 13 , 20 ] learn self-supervised visual representations without text supervision and preserve fine-grained visual structure and local semantic information. DreamSim [ 5 ] combines multiple pretrained visual embeddings together with human similarity annotations, leveraging both global semantic understanding and fine-grained visual details to produce perceptual representations that closely align with human judgments. Overall, most existing evaluation protocols are designed for static personalization settings and do not measure identity preservation or forgetting over time. 3 Evaluating Continual Performance Evaluating continual text-to-image personalization requires measuring not only the quality of generated images but also how well previously learned concepts are preserved throughout sequential adaptation. Unlike discriminative tasks, where forgetting can be directly quantified through accuracy, there is no canonical notion of forgetting for generative models. As discussed in Section 2.3 , existing evaluation protocols are primarily designed for static personalization settings and focus on aggregate measures of text or image alignment. In order to assess the degradation of the concept identity over time, it is important to have metrics that distinguish concept fidelity from general image quality. To address this problem, we first introduce a concept-level fidelity measure that quantifies how faithfully a personalized concept is preserved. We then derive continual evaluation metrics directly from this quantity. 3.1 Concept Fidelity Our objective is to evaluate the personalized concept itself rather than the similarity between individual images. A generated image may differ substantially from its reference in pose, background, or artistic style while still faithfully depicting the same concept. We therefore introduce concept fidelity , which measures similarity at the concept level rather than the image level. To quantify concept fidelity, we first measure similarity between individual generated and reference images in a learned embedding space. Given an embedding function F ⁡ ( ⋅ ) F(\cdot) , we define the similarity between two images i 1 i_{1} and i 2 i_{2} as sim ⁡ ( i 1 , i 2 ) = cos ⁡ ( F ⁡ ( i 1 ) , F ⁡ ( i 2 ) ) . \mathrm{sim}(i_{1},i_{2})=\cos\left(F(i_{1}),F(i_{2})\right). (1) While image similarity is defined between individual image pairs, the fidelity of a personalized concept should be assessed from a set of generated images rather than a single sample. We therefore generalize the image-level similarity measure by aggregating pairwise similarities across the generated and reference image sets. Let G = { g 1 , … , g m } G=\{g_{1},\dots,g_{m}\} denote the generated images corresponding to a personalized concept and let I = { i 1 , … , i n } I=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{n}\} denote the associated reference images. The concept fidelity score is defined as S ⁡ ( G , I ) = 1 | G | ​ | I | ​ ∑ g ∈ G ∑ i ∈ I sim ⁡ ( g , i ) . S(G,I)=\frac{1}{|G||I|}\sum_{g\in G}\sum_{i\in I}\mathrm{sim}(g,i). (2) This concept fidelity score extends image-level similarity to a set of generated images, providing a single measure of how well a model preserves a personalized concept. We consider several pretrained embedding models, including CLIP [ 16 ] , DINO [ 20 ] , and DreamSim [ 5 ] , as candidates for computing concept fidelity. DreamSim retrieves images belonging to the same personalized concept despite variations in pose and background, whereas CLIP and DINO retrieve visually similar images from different concepts. Let N N denote the total number of concepts. For concept k k , let G k ( T ) G_{k}^{(T)} denote the generated images after all concepts have been learned. Final concept fidelity. We define the average forgetting trajectory at training stage t ≥ t k t\geq t_{k} as F ⁡ ( t ) = 1 n t ​ ∑ k = 1 n t [ S ⁡ ( G k ( t k ) , I k ) − S ⁡ ( G k ( t ) , I k ) ] , F(t)=\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{k=1}^{n_{t}}\left[S\left(G_{k}^{(t_{k})},I_{k}\right)-S\left(G_{k}^{(t)},I_{k}\right)\right], (4) where n t n_{t} is the number of concepts that have been learned by stage t t . The trajectory measures the average loss of concept fidelity as new concepts are acquired. The final forgetting is defined as F = F ⁡ ( T ) , F=F(T), (5) which measures the average loss of concept fidelity after continual training. Together, Q Q summarizes the model’s average concept fidelity after continual training, while F ⁡ ( t ) F(t) characterizes the forgetting dynamics throughout sequential adaptation. 4 Residual-Space Adaptation in Diffusion We build upon the residual-space adaptation framework DyRA [ 1 ] , originally designed for LLMs, which constructs layer-wise adaptation subspaces from the input representations. Applying this framework to diffusion models is nontrivial, as these representations depend not only on the input concept but also on the randomly sampled diffusion noise and denoising timestep. We therefore first review the residual-space adaptation procedure and then develop a stochastic interpretation that justifies applying the framework to diffusion models and motivates our implementation. 4.1 Background: DyRA We consider a sequence of concept personalization tasks { 𝒟 t } t = 1 T \{\mathcal{D}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} , where each task introduces a new concept t t and training is performed sequentially. Following [ 1 ] , each adapted layer l l is parameterized by a LoRA update Δ ​ W t ( l ) = A t ( l ) ​ B t ( l ) , \Delta W_{t}^{(l)}=A_{t}^{(l)}B_{t}^{(l)}, (6) where B t ( l ) B_{t}^{(l)} is initialized before training and kept fixed, while only A t ( l ) A_{t}^{(l)} is optimized. The accumulated model after task t t is W t ( l ) = W ( l ) + ∑ i = 1 t Δ ​ W i ( l ) . W_{t}^{(l)}=W^{(l)}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}\Delta W_{i}^{(l)}. (7) The key idea of DyRA is to restrict learning to feature directions that are informative for the current task while avoiding directions already captured by previous tasks. For each adapted layer, the method applies a spectral decomposition of the input features matrix from all tasks, and identifies therein directions unique to the current task, i.e. the residual space leftover from previous tasks. Since different layers exhibit different residual-space spectra, the number of informative directions also varies, motivating adaptive rank allocation instead of a fixed LoRA rank. Concretely, the procedure for each adapted layer consists of three steps: 1. Estimate the input subspace most representative of previous tasks, named ℳ t − 1 ( l ) \mathcal{M}_{t-1}^{(l)} . 2. Project the current task input space ℋ t ( l ) \mathcal{H}_{t}^{(l)} onto the orthogonal complement of ℳ t − 1 ( l ) \mathcal{M}_{t-1}^{(l)} to obtain the residual space. 3. Initialize the LoRA down-projection matrix B t ( l ) B_{t}^{(l)} in the residual space, picking only directions with singular values above a given threshold τ \tau . During training, B t ( l ) B_{t}^{(l)} remains fixed and only the corresponding up-projection matrix A t ( l ) A_{t}^{(l)} is optimized. Importantly, it is the threshold which implicitly determines the layer-wise rank. This is the key to flexible rank allocation. 4.2 A Stochastic Formulation for Diffusion A key step of residual-space adaptation is constructing the residual space from layer input representations collected before training each task. For deterministic backbones, this procedure is well defined since each training sample corresponds to a unique layer input. Diffusion models, however, introduce an additional source of stochasticity through the sampled diffusion noise and denoising timestep, so the layer input of a training sample is no longer unique. This raises the central question of this section: how should the layer input space ℋ t ( l ) \mathcal{H}_{t}^{(l)} be estimated for residual-space construction? Since the optimization objective is defined over the training distribution of diffusion noise and denoising timesteps, the collected layer inputs should provide an empirical estimate of the same distribution. Therefore, layer inputs are collected using exactly the same sampling strategy as diffusion training, namely Gaussian noise with uniformly sampled denoising timesteps. This simple step extends residual-space adaptation from deterministic feature representations to stochastic diffusion training by aligning the feature collection procedure with the stochastic optimization objective. Detailed implementation and derivation are provided in Appendix B . 5 Stable Continual Personalization This section evaluates whether residual-space adaptation can be successfully extended to continual diffusion personalization. We first assess its ability to preserve concept fidelity while mitigating forgetting throughout continual learning, and then examine scalability and capacity preservation. 5.1 Experimental Setup We conduct all experiments on Concept101 [ 10 ] , a benchmark containing 101 concepts spanning 17 semantic classes, including visually similar concepts, making it particularly suitable for studying interference and identity preservation in continual learning. All concepts are learned sequentially in a rehearsal-free setting, where only the current concept data are available during training. Unless otherwise stated, all methods follow the same randomly shuffled task ordering. Throughout the experiments, we denote DyRA configured with the sigular value threshold τ \tau as DyRA- τ \tau . We compare DyRA with τ ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{0.5,1.0\} against three continual LoRA baselines: Trainable-AB , which optimizes both LoRA projection matrices A , B A,B and corresponds to a continual variant of Mix-of-Show [ 7 ] ; Rank-Fixed-B , which optimizes only the LoRA up-projection A A while keeping the randomly initialized down-projection B B fixed; and OA , the continual version of Orthogonal Adaptation [ 14 ] . Unless otherwise specified, all methods adapt the linear projections in the transformer blocks of both the text encoder and the UNet, and all fixed-rank methods use rank r = 4 r=4 . All experiments are conducted on Stable Diffusion v1.5 [ 17 ] . Models are periodically evaluated throughout continual training. For each concept, images are generated using only the learned concept token as the prompt, without additional textual descriptions, thereby isolating the learned concept representation and enabling a direct comparison of concept fidelity across methods. At the end of training, we further validate the model using diverse prompt templates. Additional implementation details and training hyperparameters are provided in Appendix C . 5.2 Concept Fidelity and Forgetting Quantitative Results. In contrast, Rank-Fixed-B and OA effectively suppress forgetting but achieve slightly lower concept fidelity. DyRA maintains negligible forgetting while achieving the highest concept fidelity. These results demonstrate that residual-space adaptation extends effectively to the stochastic training process of diffusion models. We therefore compare DyRA with the fixed-rank OA under different trainable parameter budgets to evaluate the effectiveness of dynamic rank allocation. Figure 5 compares concept fidelity against the number of trainable parameters for OA with different fixed ranks and DyRA with different singular-value thresholds. Each point corresponds to a different parameter budget. Across the entire range of budgets, DyRA consistently achieves higher concept fidelity than OA with comparable numbers of trainable parameters, demonstrating a superior performance–parameter trade-off. Figure 5 : Parameter-efficiency frontier comparing concept fidelity and trainable parameter count for OA and DyRA variants. Error bars indicate one standard deviation over three random seeds. Notably, even under high singular-value thresholds, where DyRA has substantially fewer trainable parameters, it outperforms OA with considerably larger parameter budgets. These results indicate that allocating rank adaptively according to the residual-space structure is substantially more parameter-efficient than assigning a uniform rank to every layer, allowing DyRA to maintain strong concept fidelity under a reduced parameter budget. 6 Layer-wise Specialization Section 5 demonstrated that DyRA achieves strong continual personalization performance while improving parameter efficiency through adaptive rank allocation. Beyond these empirical gains, the adaptive ranks themselves provide a signal of where adaptation capacity is consumed during continual learning, since additional rank is allocated only when new concepts introduce directions outside the accumulated input subspace. This section analyzes these rank dynamics to understand how adaptation capacity is distributed across the layers and how this information can inform future parameter-efficient adaptation. 6.1 Adaptation Capacity Concentration We first analyze how DyRA distributes adaptation capacity across the adapted layers by averaging the allocated ranks over all 101 concepts. Figure 6 illustrates the average rank allocated to each layer. The x-axis indexes the adapted layers in architectural order, and the corresponding module names are provided in Appendix D . Rather than allocating the same rank to every layer, DyRA exhibits clear layer-dependent allocation patterns that closely follow the repeated transformer architecture. In the text encoder, the allocated ranks exhibit a four-layer periodicity that exactly mirrors the repeated key(K), value(V), query(Q), and output projection layers within each transformer block. A similar correspondence is observed in the UNet, where every group of eight adapted layers corresponds to the self-attention and cross-attention projections within a transformer block. Within every block, the two dominant rank peaks consistently coincide with the cross-attention key(K) and value(V) projection layers, which repeatedly receive substantially larger ranks than all other projections. The repeated concentration of residual rank in the UNet cross-attention K,V projections indicates that these layers consistently consume more adaptation capacity than other adapted modules during continual concept personalization. This observation motivates a closer examination of these layers in the following analysis. Figure 6 : Average allocated rank per adapted layer over 101 concepts. 6.2 Early Capacity Saturation The UNet cross-attention K,V projections receive the largest residual ranks. We next examine whether exhausting the residual capacity of these layers is associated with degraded adaptation to subsequently learned concepts. Figure 7 summarizes the remaining rank of every adapted layer after learning all 101 concepts. Under DyRA- 0.5 0.5 , all 32 UNet cross-attention K,V projections become fully saturated, whereas no UNet layer saturates under DyRA- 1.0 1.0 . Figure 8 further illustrates representative remaining-rank trajectories. While non-saturated layers retain sufficient residual capacity throughout training, representative cross-attention K,V layers under DyRA- 0.5 0.5 steadily exhaust their available rank and become saturated around tasks 77–78. In contrast, the corresponding layers under DyRA- 1.0 1.0 retain residual capacity throughout the entire task sequence. Figure 7 : Remaining rank capacity after 101 tasks. DyRA- 1.0 1.0 maintains essentially unchanged performance on later concepts, whereas DyRA- 0.5 0.5 exhibits a clear late-task fidelity degradation after the cross-attention K,V layers become saturated. Although this evidence is correlational, the consistent agreement between the rank allocation, capacity saturation, and late-task performance suggests that preserving residual capacity in the UNet cross-attention K,V projections is important for sustaining continual concept adaptation over long task sequences. This suggests that these layers differentiate newly learned concepts through distinct adaptation directions. If this interpretation is correct, restricting adaptation to the identified layers would be expected to preserve most of the continual personalization performance while substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. Table 3 supports this hypothesis. Restricting adaptation to only the UNet K,V projections reduces the trainable parameter count by approximately 60% (67.56M → \rightarrow 27.12M) while achieving virtually identical concept fidelity ( Q = 0.6496 Q=0.6496 vs. 0.6497 0.6497 ) and comparable forgetting. Restricting adaptation further to only the UNet cross-attention K,V projections reduces the trainable parameter count by approximately 72% (67.56M → \rightarrow 18.87M), yet still preserves nearly all continual personalization performance in practice. Beyond validating the proposed interpretation, these results also provide a structural explanation for previous personalization methods such as Custom Diffusion [ 10 ] and C-LoRA [ 22 ] , which restrict adaptation to cross-attention K,V projections based primarily on empirical observations of large weight updates during training. In contrast, residual-space dynamics explain the same design choice from the perspective of feature-space utilization, providing a principled interpretation of why these layers are particularly effective adaptation targets. More broadly, residual-space dynamics provide a principled way to identify where adaptation capacity is most effectively utilized. Rather than relying on empirical heuristics or exhaustive layerwise search, the proposed analysis directly guides targeted adaptation, enabling substantially more parameter-efficient continual personalization while preserving nearly the same overall performance. Values are mean ± \pm SD over three seeds. 7 Conclusion Limitations and Future Directions. Although DyRA achieves strong continual personalization performance, several limitations remain. First, the adaptation capacity of residual-space methods is fundamentally bounded by the width of individual layers. As continual learning progresses, layers with consistently high adaptation demand may eventually exhaust their available residual subspaces, limiting scalability to arbitrarily long task sequences. Second, the method is implemented only on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and Concept101. Nevertheless, the residual-space analysis developed in this work is considerably more general than the specific adaptation algorithm. Since it relies only on layer input statistics and residual-space dynamics, it can potentially be applied to other diffusion backbones, transformer-based generative models, or broader neural architectures to identify the layers that contribute most to learning new tasks. Exploring these adaptation patterns across architectures may provide further insights into representation specialization and guide the design of future parameter-efficient adaptation methods. Key Takeaways. Our work shows that residual-space adaptation extends naturally to stochastic diffusion models, enabling continual concept personalization with stable performance, negligible interference, and strong parameter efficiency. Beyond its empirical performance, the residual-space dynamics observed during continual adaptation reveal how adaptation demand is distributed across the adapted layers. By identifying the layers that consistently require new concept-specific adaptation directions, it provides a structural interpretation of existing adaptation strategies and directly guides more parameter-efficient adaptation. We hope this perspective motivates future work that uses adaptation dynamics not only to improve continual learning algorithms, but also to better understand layer specialization in modern generative models.
